items.body: Ska and rocksteady set the tempo on “Be Who You Are”, a faster footing than the roots rhythms Macka B ordinarily records over, and he toasts across it in the measured address that has defined his delivery since the early 1980s. The single was released on 21 August, composed and produced by the Hamburg musician Paul Lupa, who plays keyboards and bass and surrounds them with a live rhythm section: Big Finga on drums, Robert “Dubwise” Browne on guitar, Tribuman on horns. The horns carry the melodic line, the guitar marks the offbeat, and the vocal sits forward in the mix, with the phrasing of a lyric Macka B wrote himself, vocal melody included. What he tells the listener is to be who they are. Advice has been his line of work for forty years. He has been called “the Teacher” since the 1980s for songs about what to eat, how to look after yourself and how to treat other people, and the Wha Me Eat Wednesdays vegan raps he began posting in 2017 carried that voice far beyond the reggae circuit. Lupa has been building his Hamburg catalogue around Jamaican and German vocalists since 2022, and Macka B is the most established voice to record over one of his rhythms so far. items.body: “Yira Ye” takes its title from a Bambara phrase that means roughly “that’s how it is”, and it is the first single from L’Ombre du Croco, the debut album  Bamako Express release through Trad Records on 30 October. The Ghent quartet pairs two Belgian folk players, violinist Anouk Sanczuk and guitarist Florian De Schepper, with Malian balafonist and singer Joël Massa Diarra and Burkinabè percussionist Ousmane Dembélé on djembe and calabash. Their songs are sung in Bambara. Over the past year they have played concert stages and the balfolk nights of Flanders, where couples dance to live folk bands, and in 2026 they won Best Live Band at the Flanders Folk Awards. At a balfolk night the violin carries the tune for the dancers, and in Mande music the balafon does much the same job; “Yira Ye” passes the melody between the two over Dembélé’s djembe. The track moves from quiet melodic passages into full dance rhythm, and De Schepper steps forward for a guitar solo, recorded with the rest of the song by Jeroen Geerinck at Studio Trad. items.body: Ministry released “Singularity” on September 18, 2026 through Cleopatra Records, the third single from the industrial band’s final studio album, “Hate To Go (Take Out Or Delivery)“, due October 30. The track follows the earlier singles “Burned Out” and “We Hate” from the same record. “Singularity” takes on artificial intelligence, built around a warning voiced by a cyborg character: “Your time on this planet has passed […] we are in control.” A press release ties the song to recent public alarm over AI, describing it as Al Jourgensen and the band’s timely take on the subject. The music video was directed by Ben Garcia of Rage4Order Designs, working with Jourgensen and Joshua Bradford, a former Revolting Cocks bandmate who also directed the videos for “Burned Out” and “We Hate.” Where ‘Singularity’ sits on ‘Hate To Go (Take Out Or Delivery)’ “Singularity” is track eight of ten. The album closes with “We’re Still Here”, the only track to feature former Ministry bassist Paul Barker, alongside the band’s current lineup of guitarists Monte Pittman and Cesar Soto, bassist Paul D’Amour, sampler and synth player John Bechdel, and drummer Pepe Clarke Magaña. “Hate To Go (Take Out Or Delivery)” arrives on vinyl, CD, cassette and digital formats, plus four vinyl variants (Green & Black Splatter, Silver & Black Splatter and Coke Bottle Green LPs) and two box sets pairing a splatter or marble LP with a picture LP, 7-inch and CD. Track seven, “The White Man Lied”, is left off the cassette and vinyl pressings. The full tracklist reads: Crickets Voices of Hate Clown Car We Hate Delete Grifter The White Man Lied Singularity Burned Out We’re Still Here (feat. Paul Barker) The album is available for preorder through Cleopatra Records. Ministry ‘Goodbye Europe’ tour dates 2027 Ministry closes out its career with a farewell touring cycle. Before the European leg, the band plays its remaining 2026 US and international dates: September 20 at Louder Than Life in Louisville, October 3 at the Salt Shed in Chicago, and October 24 at Sick New World Texas in Fort Worth, followed by Australia’s Good Things Festival in December with new side shows in Sydney and Adelaide. The “Goodbye Europe” tour, with Die Krupps as special guests, opens in Utrecht on April 2, 2027 and closes in Helsinki on May 1: April 2, 2027 – Utrecht, Netherlands April 3, 2027 – Saarbrücken, Germany April 4, 2027 – Brussels, Belgium April 6, 2027 – Manchester, UK April 7, 2027 – Dublin, Ireland April 9, 2027 – Nottingham, UK April 10, 2027 – London, UK April 12, 2027 – Paris, France April 14, 2027 – Madrid, Spain April 15, 2027 – Barcelona, Spain April 17, 2027 – Lausanne, Switzerland April 18, 2027 – Munich, Germany April 19, 2027 – Vienna, Austria April 21, 2027 – Prague, Czech Republic April 22, 2027 – Warsaw, Poland April 24, 2027 – Berlin, Germany April 25, 2027 – Hamburg, Germany April 26, 2027 – Copenhagen, Denmark April 27, 2027 – Oslo, Norway April 29, 2027 – Stockholm, Sweden May 1, 2027 – Helsinki, Finland A full US leg of the farewell tour has not yet been announced. About Ministry Ministry was formed in Chicago in 1981 by Al Jourgensen, a pioneering figure in industrial music. The project started with synth-pop material issued as four 12-inch singles on the newly founded Wax Trax! Records before the debut album “With Sympathy” on Arista Records in 1983. Jourgensen moved the band toward a harsher, sample-driven sound across “Twitch” (1986), “The Land of Rape and Honey” (1988) and “The Mind Is a Terrible Thing to Taste” (1989), then reached its widest audience with “Psalm 69: The Way to Succeed and the Way to Suck Eggs” (1992), which brought the first of six Grammy nominations. Paul Barker played bass and co-produced through that period before leaving the band in 2003. Eight further albums followed before Jourgensen shut the band down in 2013. Ministry returned in 2018 with “AmeriKKKant”, then issued “Moral Hygiene” (2021) and “HOPIUMFORTHEMASSES” (2024), its 16th studio album. In March 2025 the band released “The Squirrely Years Revisited” on Cleopatra Records, a set of re-recorded songs from its early synth-pop catalogue, and followed it with first-ever official videos for “Everyday Is Halloween” and “I’ll Do Anything For You” and a Jurgen Engler remix of the live track “Dancing Alone” in March 2026. Alongside Ministry, Jourgensen has run Revolting Cocks, Lard, Pailhead and Surgical Meth Machine; Barker returned to recording as Lead Into Gold in 2023. Across 45 years, Ministry has released 17 studio albums, 8 live releases and 8 side projects, toured five continents, and published an autobiography and two documentaries. “Hate To Go (Take Out Or Delivery)” closes that catalogue as the band’s final album, and “Singularity” is its third single.

items.body: US goth-industrial artist EVA X released the single “Dance in Shadows” on 18 September 2026, alongside the announcement of her second album, “TURBOPINK”, due 6 November. The single mixes synthpop, metal, power pop and 80s-referencing production, and comes backed with a breakbeat remix by Stoneburner. “Dance in Shadows” was written by EVA X collaborator Gaby Gustafson after a co-worker and friend died of an aggressive form of cancer. “I had written a super sad song originally, but I knew she’d hate that. It was really important to her to find joy wherever she could. So I ended up reworking the track into Dance in Shadows, our happy little song about death,” Gustafson stated. The B-side carries a breakbeat remix of the track by Stoneburner. EVA X’s ‘TURBOPINK’ album due 6 November “TURBOPINK” follows EVA X’s debut album, “I Dream of a Reality”, released on Distortion Productions in 2022. “Dance in Shadows” serves as the album’s preview single. EVA X returns with a full band for the touring cycle around the new record. About EVA X EVA X began as a bedroom producer, releasing her first tracks in 2019 and building a following in the goth and industrial scene through a fusion of synthwave, industrial, power pop and metal elements. Her debut album, “I Dream of a Reality”, came out on Distortion Productions in 2022 and appeared on several “best of 2022” year-end lists. She has performed at New Jersey’s Dark Force Fest, Seattle’s Mechanismus Festival and Calgary’s Terminus. Side-Line previously covered her single and video “Dopamine Blind” (2024) and her video “Machine” (2021). With “Dance in Shadows”, EVA X previews her second album, “TURBOPINK”, out 6 November 2026.

items.body: US goth-pop project Metamorph released the single “Witchfire” and its official video on 18 September 2026. The track is produced by Erik Gustafson and pairs dance-oriented beats with hook-driven melodies, alongside an extended dance mix featuring a flute solo from vocalist Margot Day. The “Witchfire” video was filmed by Brian Wimer in New York’s East Village, where Margot Day lived and performed with The Plague in the 1980s, and in the forests of Vermont. It features Day alongside bandmate Kurtis Knight. The extended dance mix, which includes Day’s flute solo, will get its own video at a later date. Metamorph’s release history Metamorph is the project of Margot Day, a New York vocalist, flutist and songwriter who fronted The Plague during the 1980s NYC goth scene alongside drummers Nick Ferrell (Spahn Ranch) and Damian (Misfits). Earlier in her career, Day played in Slow Walk 13 alongside Adam Yauch of the Beastie Boys. Formed in 2016, Metamorph blends gothic atmosphere, dark synth textures and pop songwriting built around Day’s vocals and flute playing, with Kurtis Knight providing dark synths and backing vocals on stage. Metamorph’s back catalogue includes the album “Kiss of the Witch” (2022), the album “Hex” (2024) and the retrospective “Haunted Hearts XIII” (2025), all produced by Erik Gustafson. The project has released remixes by Leaether Strip and Assemblage 23, and the single “Dance of a 1000 Miracles” featuring Stabbing Westward‘s Chris Hall has passed 20,000 Spotify streams. Metamorph has performed across the United States, Canada, Costa Rica and Guatemala, with music videos totalling more than 250,000 YouTube views. “Witchfire” follows Metamorph’s 2025 EP “Harlot” on Distortion Productions.

items.body: Nick Rhodes of Duran Duran produced Wendy Bevan’s new single “Sleepwalkers,” the third preview of the UK goth electro-pop artist’s album “Alone With The Unknown,” due September 18. The track pairs Bevan’s vocals with atmospheric synthesizer arrangements built around a feeling of loss without a clean goodbye, leaving the listener suspended between holding on and letting go. Bevan describes “Sleepwalkers” as a piece about two sides of the same uncertainty: “the old world that’s disappeared and the future that hasn’t arrived.” “We’re left somewhere, timeless and in between,” she said. “Sometimes we become so lost in our own dreams that we don’t see the destruction they cause, or recognize that we may be disappearing from our own lives.” On the song’s central tension, she added: “The act of not choosing can be just as violent as a bull in a china shop. While we long for a place called home, we unconsciously fill the spaces between with our own self-destructive behaviors.” “Sleepwalkers” is track nine on “Alone With The Unknown,” out September 18 on Chiaroscuro. The 13-track album, which also carries the bonus cut “Crazy Kinda Feeling,” was preceded by the singles “Innocence” in July and “Fragile Times” in August, both also produced by Nick Rhodes. The record continues Bevan’s production partnership with Rhodes, which began with the instrumental Astronomia series. About Wendy Bevan Wendy Bevan is a British singer, violinist and photographer raised in London who now lives in Los Angeles. She released the single “Love from the Moon” via Unknown Pleasures Records in 2016, alongside a parallel career as a fashion and fine-art photographer. In 2018 she began collaborating with Duran Duran’s Nick Rhodes, working between Los Angeles and London, on a series of cinematic instrumental compositions released from 2021 as the Astronomia project through Tape Modern, the label founded by Stephen Duffy and Nick Rhodes. The series opened with “The Fall of Saturn” on the spring equinox of 2021, followed by “Astronomia II: The Rise of Lyra” that June. In October 2024, Bevan released “Chromesthesia,” a five-track instrumental album, through her own Bandcamp page. She and Rhodes then returned to song-based material for “Alone With The Unknown,” due September 18, with “Sleepwalkers” as its third single.

items.body: Ghost Reflection, the dark electro and industrial project of Alexander Borsov, releases the concept album “Dark Triad” digitally on Aliens Production. The eight-track record mixes melodic lines, IDM loops and analog electronics around a horror-themed narrative. Borsov wrote, produced, designed and mastered “Dark Triad” himself. Aliens Production describes the record as “a cinematic concept rooted in horror aesthetics and rhythmic themes.” The tracklist runs “Games of psychopaths,” “Dark Triad,” “Integration of Madness,” “Infected,” “The root of evil,” “Thorny path,” “The Shattered World of Illusions” and “Order of Darkness.” Dark Triad by Ghost Reflection Ghost Reflection’s ‘Dark Triad’ concept The eight tracks move from “Games of psychopaths” through “Integration of Madness” and “The root of evil” to the closing “Order of Darkness,” a sequence built around horror imagery and rhythmic industrial and IDM production rather than a conventional song structure. “Dark Triad” first appeared under Borsov’s own Bandcamp page in September 2025 and now returns through Aliens Production as a digital release. About Ghost Reflection Ghost Reflection is one of several recording names used by Slovak producer Alexander Borsov, alongside Dark the Keeper, Darkmechanic and Stellar Dynamics, all mixing electro-industrial, noise and horror-themed dark electro elements. Borsov is also a member of the group Diverje and got his start in metal bands including Morgue, Atom, Cremation Deads, Sarcoma and Satura before moving into electronic production. Under the Ghost Reflection name, Borsov released the album “Dark Thinker” in June 2022 and the single “Dark Noise” in February 2024. “Dark Triad” followed in September 2025 and is now released digitally through Aliens Production, the Slovak dark electronics label that has operated since 1997 and hosts a roster of industrial, dark electro and EBM-adjacent acts.

items.body: Union Chapel in London stages “Vinyl Requiem 33.3” on 4 November 2026, a one-off return of Philip Jeck and Lol Sargent’s “Vinyl Requiem” to the venue where it premiered in 1993. Doors open at 18:30 and the programme starts at 19:30. Tickets are £18 plus booking fee through gigantic.com and are on sale now. The evening also marks the launch of a limited-edition double-vinyl reissue of “Vinyl Requiem” on Touch, the label Jeck was signed to from 1995 until his death in 2022. Vinyl Requiem 33.3 event details The programme centres on a full-scale projection of the 55-minute edited film of the 1993 performance, followed by a Q&A with people connected to the work and to Jeck’s creative life: Ghislaine Boddington (artistic director of the arts collective shinkansen), Mary Prestidge and Lol Sargent, the visual artist who created “Vinyl Requiem” with Jeck. Jon Wozencroft, co-founder of Touch, is also billed to take part. All profits from the night go to The Philip Jeck Foundation, a charity set up by Jeck’s family after his death to fund artists who produce experimental and creative work. Conceived by Jeck and Sargent at the start of the 1990s under the working title “The Death of Vinyl”, “Vinyl Requiem” was built for the 1993 Union Chapel performance from an 8-by-6-metre wall of 180 white Dansette record players, combined with 9 slide projectors and 2 16mm film projectors, according to Touch’s own catalogue notes. Three “Dansette operators” walked platforms in front of the record-player wall to swap discs live during the piece. The 1993 premiere was staged with the Institute of Contemporary Arts and also travelled to Ghent’s Time Festival in Belgium, later touring the UK, Austria and Belgium with support from the Arts Council. It won the Time Out Performance Award for Best Site-Specific Event in 1993. Sargent described the piece’s intent in an interview given around the time of its 20th anniversary: “What Philip and I created was an abstract expressionistic performance made in a very intuitive way to celebrate over 100 years of the mass public experience of the ‘record’. It was an art installation performance about a medium, using the medium.” Jeck, discussing the same period, was careful to separate the piece from nostalgia: “[Vinyl Requiem was not] a big mourning for records, I am not anti CD. It is a good starting point to mark this time of change from vinyl to other formats.” He also drew a direct line between his own practice and Sargent’s: “Lol uses his computer-controlled projectors as paint brushes. He paints with light which is similar to the way that I work with sound.” The critic David Toop, writing about the piece at the time, described its atmosphere in a short, often-cited line: “a mood of poignancy. Perhaps sadness is intrinsic to the medium.” About Philip Jeck and Lol Sargent Philip Jeck was born on 15 November 1952 and studied visual arts at Dartington College of Arts in Devon. After a trip to New York in 1979 introduced him to DJs including Walter Gibbons and Larry Levan, he began building compositions from old record players and vinyl in the early 1980s, initially scoring work for dance and theatre companies, including a five-year collaboration with choreographer Laurie Booth. “Vinyl Requiem”, made with Sargent for the 1993 Union Chapel performance, became his best-known work. Jeck signed to Touch in 1995 and released a run of albums on the label including “Loopholes” (1995), “Surf” (1998), “Stoke” (2002), “7” (2003), “Sand” (2008), “An Ark for the Listener” (2010) and “Cardinal” (2015). “Sand” was named the second-best album of 2008 by The Wire. He received the Paul Hamlyn Foundation Award for Composers in 2009. Jeck also collaborated with Jah Wobble, Jaki Liebezeit, David Sylvian, Janek Schaefer and Gavin Bryars, among others; his final credited recording was “Stardust”, a 2021 collaboration with Faith Coloccia. He died on 25 March 2022 in Liverpool, aged 69, following a brief illness. His family, including Mary Prestidge, subsequently established The Philip Jeck Foundation in his name. Lol Sargent is a UK visual artist who worked with Jeck on “Vinyl Requiem” from its conception, designing and hand-triggering the piece’s slide and film projections during live performances. He later oversaw the archival 55-minute edit of the 1993 film, released on DVD in 2013 with all proceeds going to The Philip Jeck Foundation. “Vinyl Requiem 33.3” reunites Sargent with the venue, the film and several of the people who worked on the original production, alongside the new Touch double-vinyl reissue of “Vinyl Requiem”.

items.body: Unter Strøm, the electronic duo of Alex Gonzales (Matte Blvck) and John Kunkel (The New Division, John Grand), release Transmission 003: Live at the Breathing Records Showcase, an independent live recording that runs a little over 84 minutes. The set documents a full Unter Strøm performance at a Breathing Records showcase and includes live versions of “Fragment” and “Stumbling” performed before either track had been released, along with several vocal tracks the duo were still developing. Unlike the project’s prior singles, “Transmission 003” is not a studio release. It is a concert recording, filmed and uploaded to YouTube, capturing the duo’s first time performing an Unter Strøm set in front of an audience. Unter Strøm test unreleased material in a live setting The showcase gave Gonzales and Kunkel their first chance to hear the project’s unreleased catalog through a full sound system and gauge a crowd’s reaction to it in real time. Kunkel described the goal behind the set: “We wanted the set to present a broad landscape of the Unter Strøm sound and show how many different places the project can go. After working on this music for over a year, it was exciting to finally experience it through a proper sound system and watch people respond to it in real time. What makes it even more exciting is that we still have a lot more in the tank that didn’t make it into the set.” Gonzales, describing what the performance meant for the duo, added: “The Breathing Records showcase was the first time we played an Unter Strøm set in front of an audience, so it felt like an important moment for us. We performed an hour and a half of entirely unreleased material, including ‘Fragment’ and ‘Stumbling’ before either song had been released, as well as several vocal tracks that we were still developing. It gave us a rare opportunity to test this body of work in a live environment and see which moments connected instinctively with the audience.” About Unter Strøm Unter Strøm is an electronic duo formed by Alex Gonzales and John Kunkel, based between Los Angeles and San Diego after years of the pair working together in earlier bands and studio sessions. The project mixes techno, melodic house and industrial electronics. Gonzales also records as Matte Blvck, the San Diego-based darkwave and industrial trio he leads with Bidi Cobra and Daniel Corrales, whose releases include “Vows,” “Pupula Duplex” and “Soulless.” Kunkel is the Los Angeles-based producer and songwriter behind The New Division, the synth-pop project he has led since the 2000s, is part of the Los Angeles group Trade Secrets, and also produces melodic house as John Grand, an alias that has appeared on Armin van Buuren’s A State of Trance and on Above & Beyond’s Group Therapy Radio. Unter Strøm debuted in 2025 with the two-track single “Breathing” before signing to Breathing Records, the label that launched with the “Inhale Vol. I” compilation in November 2025. The duo then released “Orynth” on May 15, 2026, “Fold” on June 12, 2026, “Fragment” on July 24, 2026 and “Stumbling” on August 28, 2026, the four singles that made up the “Between Forms” run. “Transmission 003: Live at the Breathing Records Showcase” now documents the live set where “Fragment” and “Stumbling” were first performed, ahead of their studio releases, alongside new vocal material the duo have yet to put out.

items.body: French print fanzine Lumières Noires has released its third issue, “Lumières Noires Fanzine N°3”, out now on Bandcamp. The zine is founded and edited by Vincent Dromard and covers underground and dark music. Printed in a run of 104 hand-numbered copies, the issue comes in A5 format with a glossy hardcover, 124 pages in color and black-and-white, perfect-bound and digitally printed. The text is in French. Lumières Noires Fanzine N°3 covers Pharmakon (harsh noise, visceral industrial – USA), Rosemary Loves A Blackberry / Diana Burkot (electronic art pop – Iceland/Russia), Jennifer Touch (dark acidwave – Germany), Ailise Blake (cosmic neofolk – Italy/France), Dermabrasion (death rock, disco punk – Canada), Madeline Goldstein (wet new wave – USA), Hilary Woods (blinding black drone folk – Ireland) and Robin Kester (psychedelic pop, electro rock – Netherlands), plus Buzzkill (coldwave, steel-hard punk – France), along with more than fifty reviews of vinyl, CD, cassette and VHS releases. Dromard, who runs the fanzine from France, described the issue as dedicated “to underground music.” About Lumières Noires Fanzine Lumières Noires is a French print fanzine covering underground and dark music, founded and edited by Vincent Dromard. Its first issue was released in March 2025 after six months of work, printed in 108 hand-numbered copies: A5 format, glossy hardcover, 112 pages in color and black-and-white, perfect-bound and digitally printed. That issue included interviews and features on artists such as Kælan Mikla and Denuit, alongside about fifty reviews of physical releases. The second issue followed around November 2025, printed in 100 hand-numbered copies in the same A5 glossy hardcover format, 116 pages in color and black-and-white, perfect-bound and digitally printed. It featured Ic3peak, Left For Pleasure, Donna Blue, Systeme Paradoxe, Blanche Biau, Dlina Volny, Babel Map, La Punta Bianca and Violent Vickie, plus fifty-four reviews of vinyl, CD, cassette and DVD releases; each order included a 40×30 cm poster. Lumières Noires Fanzine N°3, released in September 2026, is the third issue since the zine launched, and is available on Bandcamp alongside the first two.

items.body: The 21st-anniversary triple-vinyl reissue of Andy Bell’s “Electric Blue” has a new release date of December 4, 2026, according to the Erasure Information Service newsletter sent to subscribers on September 18, 2026. The accompanying 12″ vinyl single, “Love Oneself” / “Delicious”, is now scheduled for November 20, 2026. The Andy Bell reissue was previously delayed after audio issues were found in the test pressings. Newsletter editor Richard Evans wrote that the issues have since been corrected, new test pressings are due shortly, and the release has been rebooked into the pressing plant’s production queue. Stock delivered ahead of the release date will be dispatched to fulfil pre-orders as soon as it arrives. Everyone who has pre-ordered Andy Bell’s “Electric Blue” through Lexer Music will receive an MP3 version of the album while they wait, an offer that also applies to pre-orders placed via Lexer before September 28, 2026. The same MP3 offer applies to pre-orders of the “Love Oneself” / “Delicious” 12″ single. Vince Clarke contributes to new Ultravox book The same newsletter carries a mention of Vince Clarke‘s contribution to “Looking Backwards Towards The Future: The Story of Ultravox”, a book by Richard Evans due out on October 8, 2026 everywhere except North America, Australia and New Zealand, where it follows in February. Clarke was interviewed for the book about his fondness for Ultravox‘s “Systems Of Romance” album. The book is written with the cooperation of Ultravox’s surviving core members, carries a foreword by Moby, and includes additional contributions from Duran Duran’s Nick Rhodes and producer Steve Lillywhite. Signed and dedicated copies are available to order through Lexer Music. Unofficial remix and a teased new chapter The newsletter also points to a new unofficial remix of Erasure’s “Stay With Me” by an artist called Klaak, posted to YouTube, following an earlier unofficial Klaak remix of “Hideaway”. The remix is not sanctioned by Erasure, Andy Bell or Mute. Evans also teased that preparations are underway to announce “the next exciting chapter in Erasure’s story,” tied to a forthcoming new Erasure album project. About Erasure and Andy Bell Erasure are the English synth-pop duo of Andy Bell and Vince Clarke, formed in London in 1985. Clarke had previously co-founded Depeche Mode and Yazoo, and formed The Assembly, before pairing with vocalist Bell to form Erasure. The duo built a run of UK and international hits through the late 1980s and 1990s, including “Sometimes,” “A Little Respect,” “Chains of Love,” “Blue Savannah” and “Always.” Erasure’s catalogue has been the subject of ongoing reissue campaigns, including a 2024 vinyl reissue push covering ‘Tomorrow’s World’, ‘Snow Globe’ and ‘The Violet Flame’, and the duo marked 40 years of “Who Needs Love Like That” in 2025. Bell has maintained a solo career alongside Erasure, releasing the album “Ten Crowns” in 2025 and continuing to perform and record under his own name; “Electric Blue,” now reaching its 21st-anniversary vinyl reissue, is among his earlier solo releases. Clarke has continued to work outside Erasure as well, contributing to and remixing for other artists’ projects, including Doublespeak, his covers collaboration with Blancmange, announced earlier in 2026. The Erasure Information Service newsletter, edited by Richard Evans, has served as the duo and Bell’s primary direct fan-communication channel for reissue updates, solo activity and, as of this newsletter, hints toward a new Erasure album project still to be formally announced.

items.body: Cocteau Twins released their fifth studio album, “Blue Bell Knoll,” through 4AD on 19 September 1988. Capitol Records licensed the record from 4AD for North America, making it the first Cocteau Twins album to receive major-label distribution in the United States. The dream pop album turns 38 this year. Vocalist Elizabeth Fraser named the album after Bluebell Knoll, a peak in southern Utah. Guitarist Robin Guthrie produced the record and handled keyboards along with synth and drum machine programming, while Simon Raymonde played bass and keyboards. All ten tracks are credited to Fraser, Guthrie and Raymonde: the title track, “Athol-Brose,” “Carolyn’s Fingers,” “For Phoebe Still a Baby,” “The Itchy Glowbo Blow,” “Cico Buff,” “Suckling the Mender,” “Spooning Good Singing Gum,” “A Kissed Out Red Floatboat” and “Ella Megalast Burls Forever.” Fraser sang the whole album in her own constructed language. Raymonde later described the sessions as a settled period for the trio: “it really felt like a period of creativity and freedom, we were all getting on great musically and socially, Liz and Robin were about to have a baby, I was about to get married, there was lots of joy around. Very productive! It was a really fun record to make.” Fraser connected that ease to the decision to drop conventional lyrics, telling The Quietus in 2017: “I gained so much from [inventing language] […] Writing Blue Bell Knoll I had a wonderful freedom to put lyrics aside and not to worry [about people’s opinions].” The album reached number 15 on the UK Albums Chart and number 109 on the US Billboard 200, and “Carolyn’s Fingers” climbed to number two on the US Alternative Airplay chart. Promotional videos accompanied “Carolyn’s Fingers” and “Cico Buff.” The vinyl edition came in a limited gatefold sleeve, and the album was the first 4AD title issued commercially on DAT. After 4AD reclaimed the North American rights to its back catalogue, Guthrie remastered “Blue Bell Knoll” for a 2003 reissue, and the album was repressed on 180g vinyl in 2014. It streams on Spotify. About Cocteau Twins Cocteau Twins formed in 1979 in Grangemouth, Scotland, around guitarist Robin Guthrie and bassist Will Heggie, who took the band name from a song by fellow Scots Simple Minds. Guthrie met Elizabeth Fraser in Falkirk in 1981 and asked her to sing. The group signed to 4AD and issued its debut album, “Garlands,” in 1982, followed by “Head over Heels” in 1983. Heggie left that year and Simon Raymonde replaced him, arriving in time for 1984’s “Treasure.” Two albums came in 1986: “Victorialand,” recorded largely as a duo while Raymonde worked on This Mortal Coil, and “The Moon and the Melodies,” a collaboration with ambient composer Harold Budd. “Blue Bell Knoll” followed on 19 September 1988 and became the band’s first record to enter the US Billboard 200, a direct result of the Capitol licensing deal. “Heaven or Las Vegas” arrived in 1990 and closed the group’s run on 4AD; Cocteau Twins then signed to Fontana for “Four-Calendar Café” (1993) and “Milk & Kisses” (1996), and disbanded in 1997. All three have kept working since. Side-Line covered Raymonde’s Bella Union label presenting the debut album by his project Lost Horizons in 2017, Guthrie’s ‘Riviera’ EP in 2021 and his ‘Springtime’ EP in 2022, and reported that Fraser had returned with her first new material in 13 years in 2022. “Blue Bell Knoll” turns 38 this year, the record that opened the American market to the band two years before its 4AD run ended.

items.body: Parissior is a Spanish project founded by DJ and producer Jesu Aparicio. With “Human Control”, he releases his debut album, featuring ten tracks (although the vinyl edition contains only eight). While several EPs were released previously, this album consists entirely of new material, exploring themes such as digital identity, illusion, authenticity, and human imperfection. Musically, this translates into a very solid mix of Dark-Techno and EBM. The basslines sound menacing and pure EBM, while the kicks reveal clear Techno influences. There are also a few additional influences, such as Acid sequences, as well as some delightful old-school Techno elements that remind me of the Frankfurt scene of the 1990s. The way everything is put together sounds intelligent and, naturally, highly dancefloor-oriented. There are also some vocals worth mentioning, including a track featuring guest vocalist Jorge Tornin, although the vocals are not necessarily the most striking aspect of the album. “Human Control” is a very strong release that delivers a perfect blend of nostalgic moments and a more contemporary sound, in which Dark-Techno and EBM are inseparable and form a powerful cocktail. An album you absolutely must discover! (Rating:8½). Listen to “Eco Machines”: Eco Machines by Parissior About Parissior Parissior is the alias of Spanish DJ and producer Jesu Aparicio. He has released singles and EPs since at least 2016, including “Could I Drown In Your Desire” and “Dance To The Groove” (Spa In Disco), followed by “Let Them Dance” (Hot Digits Music, 2017) and further EPs and compilation appearances for Golden Soul Records. From “Back To Earth” (2020) onward he has worked mainly with the Espacio Cielo label, releasing further singles, EPs and compilation tracks including “Battle Cry” (2021), “Raver In The Booth” and “Full of Stars” (2023), and the Skylax release “Antennae” (2024). “Human Control” is his first full-length album.

items.excerpt: On " Chant ", another sculptor of silence shows her art. The magician is Magda Mayas, whose explorations of the outside and inside of her piano keeps astonishing us, including her inventiveness to create unheard sounds. Mayas is not only a musician, but also an academic researcher with several publications to her name, getting her PhD on the subject of " Orchestrating Timbre – Unfolding Processes of Timbre and Memory in Improvisational Piano Performance" (2019/20), which examines improvisation t
items.body: On " Chant ", another sculptor of silence shows her art. The magician is Magda Mayas, whose explorations of the outside and inside of her piano keeps astonishing us, including her inventiveness to create unheard sounds. Mayas is not only a musician, but also an academic researcher with several publications to her name, getting her PhD on the subject of " Orchestrating Timbre – Unfolding Processes of Timbre and Memory in Improvisational Piano Performance" (2019/20), which examines improvisation through timbre, space, movement, objects, and listening. I'm adding a few videos here to show her art. The first is an exercise that Magda Mayas developed for the Hochschule Luzern called " Thinking Silent Matter ". The excercise focuses on improvisation in a large ensemble context, bringing attention to silence and reduced sound material with slowly changing parameters, starting with the relevant quote : "... silence not only as absence of sound, but also silence as part of the sound" . In the video she guides her students through the concept of the exercise. Indeed, silence matters. It is even essential to anything we hear, whether we are aware of it or not, so why not actively use it in music? On the tree pieces of the album, she shows this in very different formats. The first and last piece were recorded in Australia, with two years apart, the middle track was recorded in Berlin in Tony Buck's Brief Sand Studio. The opening track, “ Embodied ,” recorded live at the SoundOut Festival in Canberra in February 2025, establishes its language through restraint. The piano notes arrive slowly, and the silences between them are as significant as the sounds themselves. Rather than functioning as a conventional prelude, however, this spaciousness becomes the central compositional device. Against the sparse piano framework, elusive sounds emerge from objects and tools used to activate the strings, producing a shifting field of resonance whose sources remain deliberately indistinct. The music is notably sparse, but never static; its intensity lies in the sustained concentration with which each sound occupies the space. “ Halcyon ” extends this approach while pushing the sonic material into considerably harsher territory. Carefully paced piano chords are subjected to feedback from a guitar amplifier, alongside a guitar pickup and various other objects. The amplification and feedback transform the piano’s familiar timbre, extending each chord into a dense, sustained resonance. Despite the expanded textural palette, the harmonic language remains remarkably focused: pitches occupy a restricted register and coalesce around a clear tonal centre. This tension between harmonic simplicity and increasingly abrasive resonance gives the piece its mesmerising quality. Developed in 2023 during the Harringtons Lane artist residency in New South Wales, “ Chant ” approaches the piano from yet another angle. The piece’s playback was recorded on sixteen different pianos, foregrounding variations in tuning and the subtle differences between instruments. Its structure is deceptively simple, built around the quiet repetition of two chords whose minute variations in tuning and timbre continually alter their perceptual weight. The effect is both soothing and strangely intense. Through repetition, small shifts become magnified, turning what might initially appear static into something constantly in flux. Across these three works, there is a consistent interest in reducing musical materials to their essentials while expanding the possibilities of resonance, texture and perception. The music derives much of its power from this paradox: the means are often minimal, yet the listening experience is anything but. What emerges is an aesthetic that feels simultaneously rigorous and intuitive—fresh, inventive and deeply attentive to the physical properties of sound. The title piece was also performed by Mayas at Roulette, streamed live on 30 Apr 2024. The video gives a great insight in her music but also on the added ingredients in the interior of her piano, things you can assume when you see a concert, but can usually at best only guess at. Enjoy! Listen and download from Bandcamp . Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body:
Eight years can change a lot. For Khalid, it has meant new albums, new stories, a stronger sense of self, and perhaps most noticeably when he steps onstage, a newfound confidence.

The multi-platinum singer-songwriter first broke through with 'Location', released just before his high school graduation, before establishing himself with American Teen and its coming-of-age anthem 'Young Dumb & Broke'. Since then, his catalogue has grown to include Free Spirit, Sincere, and most recently After the Sun Goes Down, while collaborations with the likes of Billie Eilish, Normani, Halsey, Marshmello, and Benny Blanco have further expanded his reach across pop and R&B.

Now, Khalid is preparing to reconnect with Singapore fans at It's Always Summer Somewhere Tour on 24 November at The Star Theatre, presented by Live Nation Singapore. The show marks his first performance in the country since 2018, following a planned 2020 return that did not go ahead because of the pandemic.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Bandwagon Asia | Music News • Asia Festivals & Artists (@bandwagonasia)

For Khalid, that long absence only means he has more of himself to share this time around.

“It's incredible,” he tells Bandwagon. “To be able to come back to a place that is so, so far from where I've grown up, where I originally live, I think is amazing. It really shows the power of music and just how far I can travel.”

There is also a touch of disbelief that so much time has passed.

“I'm even apologetic for taking so long to come back. Eight years is so long. So much life has happened since then, but it means that I have just more stories to bring with me when I come.”

A more confident Khalid

Fans who were there for Khalid's previous Singapore show might recognise the songs, but the person performing them has changed.

Asked what would surprise returning concertgoers most, Khalid doesn't point first to elaborate production or a new arrangement. Instead, he talks about confidence.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Live Nation SG (@livenationsg)

“I feel like before I might have been a little bit more timid, a little bit more shy,” he says. “And I feel like now I feel a little bit more confident in my craft, in my voice.”

That confidence translates physically, too. Today's Khalid dances more. He jumps more. And despite being eight years older, he says performing somehow makes him feel younger than before.

“I have a lot more energy, a lot more life,” he shares. “It's so interesting because I'm older than I was before, but in a way I feel so much younger than the last time that I was on that stage.”

For an artist whose music has long documented growing up in real time, that evolution feels fitting. Sincere explored the emotions that come with getting older, while After the Sun Goes Down pushed Khalid into another musical chapter through a blend of R&B, electro-pop, and ’80s-inspired synths.

The result is a live show that allows him to put that growth in front of the same listeners who may have grown alongside him.

“I'm just excited to really show my audience growth,” he says.

Soundtracking a Singapore night

The Singapore stop is expected to span Khalid's catalogue, from 'Location', 'Better', and 'Talk' to collaborations such as 'Love Lies' and 'Eastside', alongside songs from his latest chapter.

But if one After the Sun Goes Down track had to soundtrack a night out in Singapore, Khalid already knows his pick: 'Momentary Lovers'.

“I just think that the song feels very electric, and it just reminds me of nights that I've had in Singapore, just nights that I've had myself,” he says. “And I really love that song so much, and it's a fun one.”

For all the new music and personal growth, however, one of his earliest hits still holds a special place in the live experience.

If Khalid could leave the stage and join his own audience for just one song, he would choose 'Young Dumb & Broke'.

“I would love to be one of my fans when I'm experiencing that song for the first time, or maybe even the third, second, fourth, however many times,” he says.

The reason is simple: there is an energy around the song that even Khalid, from his position at the centre of the room, can feel taking over.

“It takes over me on the stage,” he explains. “So I would love to experience that song, if I could, from a fan's perspective.”

Perhaps that desire says as much about Khalid's relationship with his music as anything else. Nearly a decade into a career that has taken his songs around the world, he is still curious about what they feel like from the other side of the barricade.

Come as you are

As for what Singapore fans should wear to the show, Khalid isn't interested in imposing a complicated theme.

“My dress code is: wear whatever makes you feel comfortable,” he says. “I'm a big believer in, you know, come as you are.”

It is an invitation that reflects how he sees his audience: not as one uniform fandom, but as a collection of different people who have found something of themselves in his songs.

“What I love about my audience is there are so many different types of listeners and types of fans,” Khalid says.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Live Nation SG (@livenationsg)

And with a tour called It's Always Summer Somewhere, practicality helps.

“Feel free, feel loose. Wear something you can dance in, you can move in, you're not afraid to sweat in,” he adds. “But, you know, be you.”

Eight years after his last Singapore performance, Khalid isn't returning as the same artist who left. There is more confidence, more movement, more music, and, as he puts it, more stories.

For fans who have been waiting all this time, that might be precisely the point.

items.excerpt: After several records examining language (Pause/Stutter/Uh/Repeat), mutation (Mutate), liturgical memory (Ison), and the algorithmic logic of social media (Kitbashing), Abadir arrives at what feels like the conceptual centre of his work. items.body: After several records examining language (Pause/Stutter/Uh/Repeat), mutation (Mutate), liturgical memory (Ison), and the algorithmic logic of social media (Kitbashing), Abadir arrives at what feels like the conceptual centre of his work. The Primitivist is not simply a new collection of club tracks but a declaration of intent, rejecting electronic music’s enduring fixation with futurism in favour of a deeper engagement with the present and with the musical traditions that continue to shape it. The title is deliberately provocative. As Abadir has argued in an article for Cartography of Darkness, electronic music has spent decades equating novelty with the future, often reproducing the same cyberpunk imagery, dystopian fantasies and technological narratives inherited from the 1980s and 1990s. For him, that obsession has become a form of nostalgia masquerading as progress, one increasingly detached from the realities of communities living through war, authoritarianism and displacement. The Primitivist proposes another direction altogether: creativity rooted not in speculative futures but in sustained engagement with living musical heritage and the political urgency of the present. That shift is immediately audible. If Mutate revolved around the Egyptian maqsoum rhythm, this EP opens its vocabulary to rhythmic traditions and performance practices from across the Arab world. The opening “Habban” takes its name from the Gulf bagpipe, a celebratory folk instrument associated with communal dancing and percussion ensembles. Rather than sampling tradition as an exotic signifier, Abadir absorbs its rhythmic logic into a contemporary club framework where darbuka, khishba, mijwiz and intricate hand-clapping patterns become structural rather than decorative elements. The ecstatic propulsion of “The Primitivist” and the playful destabilisation of “Pass & Go” continue that trajectory, while the closing “This Is Not Another Maqsoum” knowingly acknowledges — and moves beyond — the rhythmic strategy that defined his previous album. What remains constant throughout Abadir’s catalogue is his concern with transformation. Each record asks a different question, yet all are linked by the same compositional impulse: taking existing sonic materials — speech, liturgy, social media, club music or regional traditions — and discovering how they can be reimagined without losing their historical or cultural specificity. The result is music that consistently resists easy categorisation. It is uncompromisingly contemporary, yet never relies on futurist rhetoric to justify its newness. In an electronic music landscape still eager to describe unfamiliar sounds as “futuristic,” The Primitivist offers a persuasive alternative. It suggests that innovation need not emerge from imagined worlds or technological fantasies. Sometimes it begins by listening more closely to the present and to histories that have always been there, waiting to be heard. photo by Omar Elkafrawy To helps us see beyond the future, we reached out directly to Abadir. The Primitivist presents itself as a rejection of electronic music’s long-standing fascination with futurism. You’ve argued that futurist narratives often reflect Eurocentric ideas of progress while overlooking the lived realities of communities experiencing war or authoritarianism. Once you reject futurism as the dominant framework, what new possibilities does “primitivism” open up for composition? Does it change the way you think about rhythm, sound design or even the social function of club music? My rejection of anything related to futurism has been going for five years, and each year it becomes more radical. I think this makes sense to me at the moment, since the future, futurism and the futuristic have been the main focus in electronic music since the 80’s (if not even before that) to identify what’s new, what’s next and the unheard for the western ears. This narrative of futurism has been already ruling for 40 years, which makes it outdated for me and repetitive to the maximum, to the point where it’s now reduced to a marketing label. It became a habit to link newness to the future, and unfortunately there has been a lack of critique to this idea, or attempts to link creativity and newness to something else other than futurism. It’s even nostalgic that futurism in electronic music is still somehow based on the same concepts, sounds and perspectives that once existed in the 80’s or the 90’s. There have been cycles of criticizing Mark Fisher’s theories, with a general claim that the future didn’t stop and “gotcha Fisher you are wrong”, because X or Y (from the global north) made “futuristic” music. Honestly, this argument is haunted by an outdated vision of what futuristic music means, it’s also haunted by the urge of futurism. That’s nostalgia for futurism (which is different from Fisher’s concept of lost futures) that used to exist decades ago. It’s paradoxical, and in that sense futurism is eating itself. But I think this sort of discussion doesn’t fit the Arabic context because we have different realities and priorities. With the exception of Afrofuturism, the futuristic narrative is escapist and out of touch with the present. It chooses progress and speed rather than understanding and facing the present. The narrative for years has been about fetishising dystopia or the other opposite, techno-optimism led by the “punchline” of “Let’s imagine a future where…” I see both narratives out of touch with reality, especially now. Being able to think like that is a kind of luxury, rather than living the hard present reality which is unfolding in front of our eyes on a daily basis. So at least, an action must be taken to change that, and actions happen in the present. Once we reach a point where present issues are kind of fixed, then we can have the time and luxury to speculate, think about the future and imagine it. More thoughts about this topic can be found in this essay I wrote last year. I chose the term Primitivism as a provocation, a way to say I’m happy I’m not futuristic, I’m busy with the present and I’m inspired by a deeply rooted music heritage. This way of thinking is definitely inspiring because making this claim means that I need to listen, revisit, read and learn a lot about music from the Arab region on the technical, cultural and historical level. During the last few years I learned a lot about Maqamat, rhythms from different parts of the Arab region. As you said, this also had an impact on sound design, because you can easily tell that the sound design in The Primitivist and my coming project is different from what’s in Kitbashing and Ison. On Mutate, the maqsoum rhythm acted almost as the album’s organising principle, whereas The Primitivist draws from a much broader range of rhythmic traditions and instrumental references from Iraq, Kuwait, Syria and Palestine. Tracks such as “Habban”, “The Primitivist” and “This Is Not Another Maqsoum” feel less concerned with hybridising genres than with rethinking the vocabulary of club music itself. How did your compositional approach change between these two records, and did moving beyond maqsoum also change the way you thought about rhythm? Usually I tend to link my projects together, as well as old and fresh ideas. What starts as a sound or an idea in one project will be revisited and developed more a few years later. You can trace that between Pause/Stutter/Uh/Repeat and Kitbashing or Ison, and between Mutate and The Primitivist. This marks the continuity of my work. Maqsoum was the center of Mutate, next to the influence of other club genres that I listen to and DJ. I wasn’t making club music before Mutate, so it made sense to me to start with a sound I’m familiar with and stuck in my memory, which is Maqsoum. It was fun mixing Jungle and Footwork or Jersey with sped up and cut up Maqsoum samples, to come up with a mutated club sound. In The Primitivist I decided to focus more on Arabic rhythms and dropping the influences of other club genres. During a 3 year period I got attracted to sounds from the countries you mentioned and I extended my knowledge to further other rhythmic patterns. The result was working with rhythmic sounds related to Dahhiya, Dabke, simulating a real drummer playing the Khishba or using the Sharbaka, which is a hand clapping technique rooted in the Arabian Gulf, especially in Kuwait. In my coming project, I’m going deeper in sound design, and more complex patterns with a focus on variations in time signatures. There is a striking tension throughout the EP between recognisable Arab instruments—mijwiz pipes, darbuka, khishba, brass timbres—and an approach to rhythm and sound design that remains uncompromisingly contemporary. As someone who has also been exploring Arabic maqamat and instrumental playing techniques in your more recent work, how do you avoid turning these traditions into cultural signifiers or markers of authenticity, allowing them instead to remain living musical materials? I think the idea is about avoiding orientalist and self-orientalist cliches, or lazy fusion, in addition to finding this common ground between the familiar and the unfamiliar, with surprise elements. Once you hear a Mijwiz or a brass synth for instance, you will get that sense of “yes I know that”, then twisting the expectations is the next crucial step. If I hear a Rast or Huzam or Bayati maqam used by an Arabic producer, I will see it as normal. But creativity appears depending on some other factors such as: the articulation and ornamentation in maqamat, the modulation between maqamat, how the producer is implementing these maqamat with drum patterns, how the sound design is made, how the arrangement is done and the structure is built. Here you have a lot of options to twist the expectations. Yet, I still admire the musicians who are maintaining old traditions as they are, because we need that now in our region more than any time before, given the external threat by the infamous pariah state, liberal capitalist “values”, A.I, the Dubaification of our region. This is the very material reality we face and we have to deal with in the present, so again, what future exactly are we talking about? Koleyet El Banat – photo by Omar Elkafrawy Your work sits at an unusual intersection of artistic practice and critical writing. As the editor of the electronic music section at Ma3azef, you’re constantly analysing how electronic music is written about, categorised and historicised. Has writing criticism changed the way you make music? Conversely, has producing records like The Primitivist made you more critical of the vocabulary and frameworks through which electronic music — particularly music from the Arab world — is discussed in western publications? My criticism towards the vocabulary and frameworks used in western publications as well as the westernised Arabic ones has always been there. I also believe that the music journalist or the critic has to read, follow and listen a lot, a good level of curiosity is required. I’m trying to do my best with that, so my critique can have some basis. Maybe The Primitivist is a result of that. It’s about how to express critique through a medium other than writing; proposing that we don’t need to be obsessed with the future or futurism to be creative, alternatively, we can be focused in the present or we can draw inspiration from our cultural roots. The present is here already. The same applies on Kitbashing by the way, one can theorise about its concept in an essay or a book, but I wanted to represent the concept sonically. Definitely, working in criticism has made me think differently about my own music, because it has made me much more self-critical. My music projects are slow cooked, and each one starts with a simple question: why am I doing this or what am I trying to say? This question can be frustrating or provocative to some artists, but for me it makes total sense and it’s the main critical question behind every project.ِ During the process, I can be very critical and harsh towards myself, but it helps me a lot. With Kitbashing, you proposed feeding on the algorithm rather than feeding it, transforming the sounds of social media into compositional material. In retrospect, do you think the algorithm can ever truly be subverted, or does every attempt at resisting it inevitably become another form of participation? On an individual level, we can benefit from the algorithm, whether by using it for learning purposes, an introduction to something, being informed about cultural or political topics, or simply watching something fun, because we need a break. Apart from that, ِI wish in general that the algorithm is subverted for something good and I think this has to be collectively done. Take for instance the non-commercial electronic music scene which is now driven by the algorithmic scrolling mentality, everyone from the curators, to the spaces, to the artists, to the press, to the crowd, is so invested in an app. Everything has been highly dependent on Instagram. It has become the main way to be heard and seen and that’s exhausting and frustrating. A couple of slides or a polished one minute video from the peak of a live or DJ set defines an artist. But imagine that the press and curators are relatively withdrawing from Instagram, this can have a good impact on producers and DJs, they will spend less time on the app, and post less, only when it’s necessary. This will make the crowd spend more time listening and reading, and artists will only focus on their music and their work. That would be ideal, isn’t it? (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Review by Progfan97402 — Another installment in the Ozric catalog and they're that rare band that never released a bad album. This is the first album in years to feature the Erpman on the cover. Harmonic Mind is exactly what you come to expect from this band, nothing more, nothing less. The usual over-the-top guitar playing from Ed and all sorts of spacy synthesizers from both Ed and Silas. Saskia Maxwell appears to be the replacement for John, and it seems Paul Hankin is hanging around as he was with the band early on and started reappearing on albums like Technicians of the Sacred onwards. "Space Platform" was the preview single and if you heard it you know it's Ozric Tentacles and no one else. The title track starts off slow and acoustic and picks up at the end. As an Oregonian I find it amusing one of the tracks is called "Tillamook". It's the name of a small coastal town, the famous cheese locally made, the county, and the local Native American tribe. I don't notice any Native American influences in the music but it's an incredible piece of Ozric space rock that only they can do, it's definitely a highlight on this album. The rest is still amazing stuff, how do they do it? If you thought the Ozrics were doing the same thing for the last 40 years I doubt this would change your mind but if you love that sound there's no reason not to give Harmonic Mind a try.

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — Well John, it was my pleasure, though my answer dates four years after your thanks. Glad you enjoythis very special project.TBH, I delayed this review, because I didn't really know what to make of this album (lasting adouble LP release plus a 45RPM single) at acquisition time. Sure, the title announces that it willbe quite a program: Vertigo of Flaws: Emancipation of the Dissonance and Temperaments in IrrationalWaveforms and it doesn't lie about the sonic contents. The Diaz brothers have widened theirsoundscapes and we find some Industrial music (very early Popol Vuh and Kluster albums aren't far) to Ozric (well almost ;-))), but it's the former trend that dominates. In some ways, it feels a bitlike scrapping the bottom of the archives drawer (not sure it is the case, though), because the duoand their guest don't try to link the different bits, and there are odd stops inside the tracks'duration.As far as the Indus side, there is nothing aurally offensive (ala Throbbing Gristle), but nothingall that pleasant either and they're grouped in two packages, separated by the usual Trees Speaksoundscapes tracks. You'll still find great spoons of spices like Tangerine Dream, Cluster, early-Kraftwerk and the hypnotic "motorik" rock of Neu! or Can in the Emancipation of the Dissonance andTemperaments in Irrational Waveforms soup. Ultimately, despite a greater sonic scope, Vertigo ofFlaws is indeed flawed and overlong, and even overstays its welcome, partly because TS fail to renewitself, despite the greater spectrum presented here. Definitely not their best effort.

And with three reviewers hailing this a "masterpiece" and referencing the band Kansas - well, I had to check this out. I consider "Leftoverture" a masterpiece, this... no. The musicans are: Lisa LaRue, composer, keys, drum and computer programming; John Baker, guitar, bass, vocals; Jake Livgreen, vocals; With... Joe Deninzon, violin, and Evan Stanley, guitar, each play on one song. So this is really a duo. The musicians are quite good and Lisa's compositions are good, but it has a Neal Morse / Flying Colors vibe more than a Kansas vibe, for me. I like that Quivira has lots of instrumental sections - where the musicians can jam - because the vocals are far from the majestic duo that was Steinhardt and Walsh. In fact, there aren't many vocals on this album at all. Overall, this is a good debut album, and if you enjoy a mostly instrumental retro 70's style of music, Quivira could be worth a listen. I'm curious is this a one-off, or is a second album with a human drummer a possibility? Solid 3.25 stars.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — During that busy yet fruitful year of 2017, following Flying Microtonal Banana and Murder of the Universe, came Sketches of Brunswick East; its title references the Melbourne suburb of Brunswick East and Miles Davis's 1960 LP Sketches of Spain. It is also a collaboration with the American group Mild High Club.It can also feel like a sequel to Paper M�ch� Dream Balloon, featuring bossa nova and an acoustic feel, yet it sets itself apart by seeming drenched in LSD, with a soft layer of psychedelia; the electric piano, drum grooves, and wah-wah guitar create a postmodern jazz-rock effect where the 60s meet the 90s and 2000s, and yet, in songs like "D-Day," it is microtonal.This album features some very interesting variations; the band experiments with pop, ranging from the array of percussion instruments to the use of vocals, backing harmonies, and the melodies themselves, sometimes with instruments following the vocals, and at other times doing the exact opposite, as seen in "Tezeta." The flute and Mellotrons create a distinctive atmosphere; combined with the 60s-style jazz they execute so well and those catchy choruses, they help shape the bohemian vibe sought in "The Spider and Me.""Sketches of Brunswick East II" introduces a recurring motif, tinged with the flamenco-esque flair that inspired it, that weaves through the entire album in various forms. When King Gizzard proposes a journey into the future, you have to buckle up; this time, however, they head into the past, embodying the roles like true method actors and channeling the musical sensibilities of that era. There is a space-age atmosphere, combined with a certain sophistication, that they capture brilliantly on "Dusk to Dawn on Lygon St." Meanwhile, "The Book" stands as another microtonal experiment; given that it was 2017, such a track was bound to make an appearance, yet it fits seamlessly with the album's playful psychedelia."A Journey to (S)Hell" offers a dose of urban chaos; just as Paper M�ch� Dream Balloon was the countryside, Sketches of Brunswick East is the city. A nocturnal journey awash in psychedelic lights unfolds suddenly, reconnecting with 70s-style synthesizers on "Rolling Stoned" before shifting to bossa nova on "You Can Be Your Silhouette." It is nearly impossible not to dance to this endless string of short songs, a fitting format, like small slides or snapshots of the city and open windows, each distinct in its own specific character."Sketches of Brunswick East III" brings the album to a close, and this peaceful interlude paves the way for the next chapter of 2017, Polygondwanaland, though that belongs to another dimension, one of the many inhabited by this Australian band.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Recorded in London at Orange Recording Studios LTD. December 9-12, 1970 and then released early in 1971 by Global Records.A1. "Thursday Morning Sunrise" (11:38) not the opening I was expecting--ever--from a 1971 prog album much less a Jazz-Rock Fusion one. The deep, low, heavily distorted organ play sounds like Markus Pajakkala's baritone saxes and bass clarinet on his (memorable) 2017 Brutopianisti album! When other instruments finally join in they're all grotesquely distorted: Eberhard's wild (and virtuosic) electric bass, Siggi Schwab's Sonny-Sharrock/Arto Lindsay-like electric guitar, even the drumming/percussion work of Fred Braceful and Roland Wittich is wild. I wouldn't call this "Free Jazz" like something from Ornette Coleman, John Coltrane's post-A Love Supreme period, or Sun Ra's Arkestra, but a fusion of these with experimental sound explorations and, in the second half, the incorporation of sophisticated African rhythms with even some from the more avant-garde realms of Classical Music. I am blown away, incredibly impressed, and find myself incredibly entertained as well as fully enjoying this trail-blazing exercise in boundary-obliteration. Could this album have been a key food source for the inspiration of soon-to-appear bands like UNIVERS ZERO or AREA?--certainly this type of music (19.25/20)A2. "Lady Blue" (3:03) now, hearing this amazing song that combines Beatnik poetry-delivery musical formats with Classical Music choral traditions, I find myself asking whether or not Wolfgang, Eberhard, Siggi, and/or Fred were fans or progeny of George Russell's School of Esoteric Musics while George was a professor in residence at Sweden's Lund University. I absolutely love this! Another totally unexpected song that I find myself returning to over and over to try to fathom its creative scope. (9.75/10)A3. "Mellodroma 2a" (5:10) more choir appearances open this--from a distance--before Siggi's acoustic guitar enters playing with congas and double bass in what can only be descrived as a Folk Rock tune akin to something by Bert and John, The Pentangle, or The Incredible String Band. And the choir continues to make small appearances! These guys are amazing! The diverse interests and forms for their musical expression seems to have no bounds! Lite drums join in but it's the hand percussion that dominates with Eberhard's double bass Wonderful! Another song that totally took me by surprise and which lures me back again and again for repeated listens as I try desperately to fathom their thinking and desires. In the fourth minute there is a lull in which Siggi gets to show off a little more of his acoustic guitar skills, but then the rest of the band re-joins for a rousing finish with percussion and organ really bringing it (though no return of the choir). Wonderful! (9.333/10)B1. "Raga" (16:17) apparently Siggi Schwab had really gotten into a huge variety of World Music stringed instruments--and especially stringed instruments prevalent in India--like the but also zithers, psaltries, This track was actually written by Siggi, who is credited with a vast array of traditional, ethnic, and Indian stringed instruments on the record. Among the highly zither-like instruments he plays on the album and track are the swarmandal (credited as "surmandel") and the bulbul tarang. Siggi also contributed sitar, veena, tambura, and sarangi to the album's rich, psychedelic raga-rock sound. Eberhard, Fred, Roland, and Wolfgang do their best to provide inputs that they think will enhance, embellish, and not detract from Siggi's reverence for his Indian studies. I find the use of the full drum kit in the seventh through ninth minute to be a bit overwhelming and domineering to the Indian spirit being expressed but, it's a good awareness experiment and, fortunately, it ends so that the song can move into a new, more-percussion-centric passage--one that contains Eberhard's talking drum like bass play as well as a lot of intertwined and improvisationally-reactive percussion threads, gradually embellished by trumpet and, later, cymbal-crashing drum kit and distorted synth string sounds. Things quite down again in the sixteenth minute, leaving Siggi and his mates to finish the song with a thin palette of almost-incidental noises and percussives to usher Siggi's surmandel out. (By the way, Fred's drum play over this last sections is much more tasteful and respectful--much less invasive and brutal.) Another surreally-unexpected and eminently-enjoyable song that makes me wish I had been there--wish I could have been present for these practice and recording sessions as well as known these remarkably intrepid musicians! (28.25/30) B2. "Milkstreets" (4:15) a relatively unstructured melange of natural and unnatural (treated and electonic) sounds, many coming from African and Indian traditions. Interesting and historically significant (like the work of John Cage, Terry Riley, Herbie Hancock, Area and so many other adventurists). (8.875/10) Total time: 40:23YouTube provided me with three extra/bonus songs that apparently came from the same December 1970 London recording sessions but only saw the light of day (and a public awareness) on a 2008 CD release from the Long Hair label. They are also quite interesting and experimental, allowing for even more display of all the weird instruments that Siggi and Wolfgang had been playing around with. A/five stars; an absolute masterpiece of experimental and leading-edge Jazz-Rock Fusion. HIGHLY recommended and ESSENTIAL for any J-R Fusion and Progressive Rock fan.

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — Rounded up to the third star.Difficult to give it more, as Strange Terrain, because it is out of topic for this site, though you will find a bit of the madness that made Mice & Rats In The Loft so excellent, but musically this is nothing alike the first two albums. Here we're dealing with some New Wave - the 80's type - but way avant-la-lettre. So much so, that one can wonder whether these two unreleased sessions (not until 2010) were indeed recorded in 77. If that had been the case, it would be considered as groundbreaking had they been released back them. I some ways, some of the early tracks on this album are fun and can even qualify as Zolo-type of rock, and 80's Sparks aren't that far either. One can think of also later (as in recent) Aksak albums with Veronique Vincent. In the meantime, one can wonder why this archives compilation was released under the JDDG moniker, since the second salvo (bonus tracks) were labeled as Noy's Band. But in either case, if you're looking for JDDG soundscapes, you're not going to find much similar, though as I said the looniness is worth a listen.
