items.body:
The brotherhood of foundational European avant garde bassists gets smaller with each passing year. And among those still living, some are either inactive for various reasons or working in other fields, musical or otherwise. So, the subset of ones still going is a small but precious list.

Among them is the Netherlands’ Arjen Gorter. Ask even a relatively informed listener of European avant garde jazz about him and almost invariably the first association will be Willem Breuker, and more specifically his Kollektief. Gorter did anchor that group for the entirety of its existence (1975-2010, with a retrospective farewell tour coming after Breuker’s death) alongside drummer Rob Verdurmen, allowing Breuker and a rotating cast of string and horn players (though trombonist Bernard Hunnekink was another stalwart) to navigate complex and subversive music, confident that a strong foundation would always support them. But like Jimmy Cobb always being referenced first and sometimes only as the last living participant of Kind of Blue after Miles Davis died in 1991, Gorter’s career, still ongoing, is hardly exclusive to his work with Breuker.

Gorter was born in Amsterdam on January 2nd, 1948 and he has resided in the Dutch capital his whole life. His road to the bass was a circuitous one. As he wrote in an email, “I liked the accordion when I was very young. It was common in the Amsterdam streets of the ‘50s, but the tunes that my teacher made me play were too silly, so that did not last. My dad imported musical instruments. He brought a slightly damaged ukulele home and so at around 11 I tried playing along with the nightly jazz broadcasts on French and Belgian radio. The father of a friend had a small jazz collection and I loved the Art Blakey Blue Note 45s, the Monk LP and the other stuff he had. So that ukulele was replaced by a guitar. I started jamming in our attic with friends and others and at some point someone brought a double bass upstairs and left it there for six months. I had fun playing it and managed to buy it from him once he showed up again.”

During high school Gorter played guitar in a band for school dances, repertoire ranging from period rock tunes to jazz compositions. He began college in 1966, aiming to study political science and sociology, the same year he first worked professionally with Breuker, having heard the older reed player’s bands around town and once playing with him at a jam session. Gorter was invited to join a new Breuker group, which performed at the Loosdrecht Jazz Competition as a sextet, then expanded to almost two-dozen musicians for the final stage. This group would make Litany for the 14th of June 1966 (Relax) in late October 1966, Gorter’s recording debut alongside two other bassists, the much older Dick van der Capellen and Victor Kaihatu.

Gorter would balance university and performing for a few years. During this time, he would work with Germany’s Gunter Hampel, appearing on his April 1968 Wergo date Gunter Hampel Group + Jeanne Lee and participating in the November 1968 Total Music Meeting in Berlin, where photo evidence has him in a bizarre encounter with Hampel, John McLaughlin, Sonny Sharrock, Pharoah Sanders, Roy Ayers, Laurie Allan, and Roel Kroes. 1969 saw even more activity: more Hampel work, including the album The 8th of July 1969 (inaugurating his Birth imprint); playing on German trumpeter Manfred Schoof’s FMP release European Echoes and being part of the Peter Brötzmann Oktett at the International Holy Hill Jazz Meeting (alongside Buschi Niebergall and Peter Kowald; Richard Williams’ review of European Echoes in the March 14th, 1970 issue of Melody Maker saying, “It’s an astonishingly powerful performance, with particularly superb work by Dudek, Bailey and the three basses, who play a really fantastic trio section.”). Gorter is also heard on the Live at The Bohemia Jazzclub recording by Hans Dulfer’s Soulbrass Inc., as well as a track with Breuker and Han and Peter Bennink heard on the Instant Composers Pool cheese box. As Gorter recalled, “I managed to juggle both activities until the end of 1969, but I was more on the road than in Amsterdam and had to make a choice and I chose the activity that gave me way more satisfaction.”

During the first half of the ‘70s, Gorter and Breuker did not work together often, at least as can be gleaned from available recordings: Hampel’s People Symphony (Birth, 1970) and part of his group that participated in German avant garde composer Hans Werner Henze’s Der Langwierige Weg In Die Wohnung Der Natascha Ungeheuer; and an unofficial Amsterdam recording from 1973 under Breuker’s leadership and a live date from Leo Cuypers in 1974, both with groups prefiguring the Kollektief (Cuypers was its first pianist). Otherwise Gorter was busy – again, at least on record – with Hans Dulfer, Kees Hazevoet, Theo Loevendie, Alexander Von Schlippenbach, and the Irène Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl Quartet. The latter two were significant. Gorter was part of the second iteration of Schlippenbach’s Globe Unity Orchestra, Niebergall and Kowald in tow once more (a 1970 Berlin Jazz Festival performance released in 2001) and the Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl group that was active for several years. “I met Rudiger in Wuppertal, that was a new jazz center by itself thanks to Peter Brötzmann and Peter Kowald,” wrote Gorter. “Sometimes I stayed at the studio that he shared with guitar wizard Hans Reichel. When Irene and Rudiger started playing together, they asked me to join and we played many places in the early ‘70s, with Heinrich Hock, Louis Moholo, or Alan Bateman on drums.” That band made only one full album, 1974’s Goose Pannée (FMP) but did have a track on the For Example - Workshop Freie Musik 1969 - 1978, the FMP boxed set.

1974-75 was an important period for two other reasons. Besides the aforementioned collaborations as well as work with the Boy Edgar Big Band and the small groups of Maurice Horsthuis and Toon van Vliet, Gorter was one of the musicians who helped establish Amsterdam’s Bimhuis, ultimately one of Europe’s premier venues for avant garde music, performing on its October 1st, 1974 opening night with the Burton Greene Quartet. Then in March 1975, Breuker asked Gorter to be a member of his Kollektief. Gorter described the group’s music as such: “Willem’s music had a lot of freedom. There were often tightly arranged written sections that would suddenly end and then the fun was to play on as if the arrangement continued – there was usually no such thing as chord changes – or to let the thing fall off a cliff ... Anyway, the music always felt fresh to play, even after many concerts, and there was a great mix of individual input and group discipline and cooperation. The Kollektief’s music linked the recognizable to the unexpected, often in 90-degree turns. It was surprising but accessible. For us musicians there was a wide spectrum of activities, from theater plays to movie music to interpretations of classical music and a lot of traveling to places where we found appreciative audiences, ranging from Australian school children to Chinese businessmen.”

The Kollektief would go on to make over three dozen albums, mostly released on Breuker’s BV Haast label, and perform all over the world, including during the Klap op de Vuurpijl (roughly, Top It All Off) Festival, taking place over five days at the end of each year from 1976-2005. Its book mixed Breuker and other band member pieces with tunes from various pages of the Great American Songbook and drawn from the classical canon, as well as other sources, presented in a highly theatrical manner best appreciated live and mixing in humor in refreshing contrast to the dour stage demeanor of many an improviser.

As busy as the Kollektief would keep him, Gorter still pursued other projects, some including fellow Kollektief members, including Breuker, and only existing on stages, such as groups under the leadership of Maarten van Norden, Sean Bergin, Boy Raaymakers, Pierre Courbois, Nedly Elstak, Jasper van ‘t Hof, Misha Mengelberg, and others. A representative sampling of those can be found in the archive of the Bimhuis (https://www.bimhuis.nl/archief); when he was in Amsterdam, this would be Gorter’s home near his home.

But there were also ones documented as albums: Maine, the 1975 collaboration of American trombonist Roswell Rudd with Dulfer, Gorter, and drummer Martin van Duynhoven, was made up of music by Sonny Rollins and Rudd (who had been coming to and working in the Netherlands since the mid ‘60s both with the New York Art Quartet and also locals like Loevendie). There were two 1977 dates by Cuypers, Zeeland Suite also including another bassist in South African expatriate Harry Miller; the 1979 Maarten Van Norden/Boy Raaymakers quartet date Chicken Song, completed by drummer Peter Nykyruj (of Mike Osborne fame); and a pair of 1980 albums spearheaded by the aforementioned trumpeter/composer Elstak (and released on his Coreco label; Gorter had loosely studied harmony with him in the ‘60s): To Build was led by Soesja Citroen’s name, who was one of five singers alongside Elstak, Breuker, Gorter, and Van Duynhoven for Sad Trumpets. The most significant, at least in terms of international exposure, came in July 1984, when Gorter, Mengelberg, and Bennink joined forces with two Americans, soprano saxophonist Steve Lacy and trombonist George Lewis, for the Soul Note release Change of Season (Music Of Herbie Nichols). Another important recording came 13 years later with Legendary: The 27th of May 1997, in a reunion with Hampel, who was fêting his seminal Heartplants SABA album from 1965 with original participants Courbois, Schlippenbach, and Schoof, Gorter standing in for his late friend Buschi Niebergall. One interesting takeaway from this is that it is often thought that after Breuker split with his fellow Instant Composers Pool founders Mengelberg and Bennink there were two distinct worlds in Dutch avant garde jazz; however, there were musicians like Gorter who operated in both spheres.

The new millennium found Gorter in several new projects: the mostly American blues/jazz band New Texas Swing from American saxophonist and then fellow Kollektief member Alex Coke with singer Tina Marsh and drummer John Betsch; the aptly named though horn-heavy Drummers Double Bill from Arend Niks and Verdurmen; 2000 recording The Compositions Of Eric Dolphy (BV Haast) with Coke, Breuker, Eric Vloeimans, Frank van Bommel, and John Engels; and Bo Van De Graaf’s I Compani; and the Rahsaan Roland Kirk “tribute” band Reeds & Deeds, also put together by Van De Graaf.

The Dolphy project had a personal resonance for Gorter, more specifically a much younger version of himself. In 1964, when he was 16, Gorter attended the Charles Mingus Sextet performance at Amsterdam’s Concertgebouw, a band with Dolphy, Johnny Coles, Clifford Jordan, Jaki Byard, and Dannie Richmond, which Gorter calls “the best ever ... Halfway through a trumpet solo by Johnny Coles, Eric left the stage while playing and walked into the hall. He ended up right next to my seat, way in the back. For a 16-year-old, that may have been a life-changing experience.” In 2011, Gorter was given the opportunity to celebrate Dolphy once more with a concert at the Bimhuis: “Eric Dolphy at The Five Spot Revisited,” with the legendary recording’s repertoire played by himself, Tom Arthurs, Rudi Mahall/Alex Coke (as his bass clarinet and saxophone/flute sides), Benoît Delbecq, and John Betsch.

Gorter joined the multimedia ensemble I Compani, founded by Van De Graaf in 1985, in 2010. As he wrote, “Bo van de Graaf just called it quits for I Compani, which I understand but regret. He led that band for 40 years through great adventures and I was happy to participate since 2010 or so. If anyone is comparable to Breuker in the amount of initiatives he took, it is him. Original pieces are blended with film music and live video, in various lineups from septet to 18-piece band. His music has the space, freedom and versatility of Breuker’s, but in a different way. Fun!”

When asked about the European scene in which he came up, Gorter replied, “At that time every European city had a very original and recognizable improvised music scene, or a few of them, like London with both the Spontaneous Music Ensemble and Brotherhood of Breath,” he wrote. “And they all had international contacts and were sharing with each other. So, the originality of these approaches, and the mutual respect, encouraged the exchange between countries and scenes and the musicians and their supporters took the initiative to made it happen.”

As for his own methodology towards, as shown in this piece, the variety of musical situations in which he has taken part, Gorter spoke both simply and profoundly: “From the beginning I played both free improvisation and tunes based on chord changes. Learning on stage was an option in the ‘60s, which sometimes led to embarrassment but more often to improvement. My approach is: first try to play what you hear, then figure out what others call it (= music theory), then apply that to play better what you hear and so on. Nowadays much education starts on the second step ...”

items.body:
This column is a loose gathering of recordings – two duos, two quartets – that might define a certain frontier, a degree of meaning in improvised interactivity spreading over 12 years. At times, the combination of close listening and simultaneous writing (the only way I can find to describe this music) results in verbal collisions that may be elusive in meaning, but they may also legitimately represent some of the transformative complexity and overlapping visions arising in these works of essentially collective invention. Though one of these recordings is more than a decade old, they may represent a kind of perpetual edge.

Certain musics can pass through walls of custom, identity, and meaning, assuming unknown shapes, escaping any strict verbal denotation, meaning becoming at once plastic and ineffable. Such music cannot be analyzed or described successfully, such failed exercises, however, perhaps contributing to both its mystery and its beauty, music that might suggest a hymn from an unknown culture, possibly disappeared, to an unknown deity, possibly deceased. In collectively improvised music, the role of the listener is paramount: assembling, collecting, composing ... At the same time, however, no interpretation is more privileged than another. These particular recordings are by musicians who can create dreams in sound. Some will imagine mills or factory floors, tuned to and amplifying unimaginable inventions of human industry. Empathy contributes a mutating, transformational soundscape. These are musics that create uncommon space.

Die Dritte Ebene (45 rpm LP, NiVuNiConnu, nvnc-lp062) by Emilio Gordoa and the late Sven-Åke Johansson might initially seem exotic. Ultimately, it’s not. It’s work of perfect transparency, that is, a view of whatever one hears as the other side of anywhere. The cover offers two titles, DIE DRITTE EBEN or EL TERCER NIVEL, “the third level,” in German or Spanish, with each phrase written with the “E”s written as reversed 3s. The phrase arises in Gordoa’s brief description appended to the Bandcamp page: “We were discussing how our music moves as if in parallel lines, and how after a while something third will emerge from it, almost like a ghost. It is something I find almost mystical: how this third level manifested itself in our playing without us thinking about it.”

Reminiscent of Johansson’s previous NiVuNiConnu release, Tea Time, with Nicholas Bussmann and Yan Jun, the music hints at Erik Satie’s Furniture Music, somehow constituting a radical background music that enhances consciousness, the special resonance of repeated materials creating a trance-like, near-ecstatic state, a reflective consciousness that rises between the parts created by Johansson and Gordoa, illuminating as well as hypnotic. Die Dritte Ebene, from August 26, 2023, points to an ineffable quality – a kind of trance, a kind of lift, a spectral point of attention that is produced in a listener’s collaboration with the close echoes, tight resonance and metallic rattle of Johansson’s snare, the reeds of his accordion, and the glassy ring of Gordoa’s vibraphone, glowing like light in sonic form. The shared insistence and simultaneity of Johansson and Gordoa’s work consistently expands what is essentially a minimalist musical environment, concluding with a strange abstraction of accordion and vibraphone that might suggest a kind of musical haunting.

Nate Wooley and Seymour Wright recorded About Trumpet and Saxophone in 2012, appearing on the Fataka label in 2013. While that release was unquestionably radical, its forthcoming successor, recorded in 2025, About Saxophone and Trumpet (Relative Pitch) takes a very different initial tack, opening with a deconstruction of the romantic ballad “The Midnight Sun,” composed by Lionel Hampton and Sonny Burke in 1947, recorded initially as an instrumental, with sufficient melodic grace to have lyrics later added by Johnny Mercer, spurring recordings by June Christy, Ella Fitzgerald, and Carmen McRae. Here the melody is clearly audible through a series of gasps, honks, and shattered, incomplete phrases, a nod to tradition that rapidly expands, becoming increasingly inclusive.

There follows “Experiment Four,” an extended dialogue which includes some of the strangest sounds ever emitted by saxophone and trumpet, often coming from very different positions in the sound spectrum. The fourth track, “Untitled,” is genuinely conversational, though the conversation is conducted in assorted bleats and blasts. Each musician is repeatedly triggered by the other’s material, whether pinching their sound inward, or adapting a radical extroversion. Music here will stand in for complex human relationships and perceptions, a sound store evolving to mark the impact of events in one’s daily life, worlds for which artists have long been refining their techniques and perceptions. As our descriptive apparatus daily fails before global events, our key artists stretch the elements. In that sense, call it modern syntactical practice or a soundtrack to Guernica, but the expressive range in which Wooley and Wright here operate seems perfectly in keeping with the daily news. Meanwhile, the inner tunings and sustained tones, even their matching fast vibratos suggest the development and synergy of an expressionist language. Sudden shifts will swiftly resemble elegant balladry of yore, echoes of that “Midnight Sun.”

While the Wooley/Wright duet recalls Fataka, Trevor Brent’s remarkable label – “‘dedicated to releasing recordings of small group and solo improvisations with a particular interest in situations where a common musical language has not yet fully emerged” – has become active again, releasing Parallels & Diagonals by a quartet from the label’s earlier period, 14th July 2014 at Cafe Oto, in which Wooley and Wright appear in a quartet with two percussionists active since the dawn of English free improvisation, Paul Lytton and Eddie Prévost. Contrary to Brent’s explanation of the label (and a genuine generational difference: the percussionists had discographies before the wind players were born), the four musicians seem so closely attuned – each a genuine spontaneous composer – that they sound like they might have had a long history together. Parallels and Diagonals is 12-year-old music, but it sounds like it might be recorded next year.

The opening track, the extended Parallel A, sounds like a machine shop that has discovered free improvisation, shifting dramatically after a passage of silence shortly after the 15-minute mark. The sounds suggest a light roll on a kettle drum, a brush on a cymbal, the sound of air pushed delicately through a trumpet. This notion of interiority marks the collective passage of these musicians, finding a terrain at once both barely imagined and yet a defining part of the human condition. In Diagonal A, fundamental gestures, like air squeezed through a metal tube, take on their own significance, behaving like Buddhist mudras, invoking fundamental gestures and symptoms of human life, murmurs, signs, abrasions. Diagonal B’s rapid actions and continuous overlapping suggest activity so closely attended by the musicians that it might follow a score in which the pauses might be carefully accounted, floating among a delicately bowed cymbal, other sounds that cannot be identified, and some that shimmer around audibility.

foam and mesh (Fundacja Słuchaj Records) by the B:A:N:S BAND is the work of pianist Sophie Agnel, saxophonist John Butcher, bassist Pascal Niggenkemper, and percussionist Ståle Liavik Solberg, recorded at the 2024 ArtAct Festival in St. Johann, Austria. While it’s the only grouping here with a conventional instrumental grouping, the orientation of the musicians will ensure that there is nothing resembling convention in the ways that the instruments are utilized.

foam and mesh I is clearly the main event, a 35-minute dialogue in which four of the most skilled spontaneous composers put together a dense weave of sonic events, with nothing predictable, yet everything interlocking. Tension curves are developed with astonishing power, each member of the quartet seemingly pursuing a unique and independent path, yet everything contributing to an astonishing rhythmic taffy-pull in which every part contribute to a compound and original overall momentum. This complex relationship will sustain through numerous group movements, whether slow balladic ruminations with isolated knocks and flurries or a sudden tense wedding of trembling oscillations, all four musicians regularly finding distinct timbres. The relatively brief foam and mesh II initially foregrounds Agnel’s piano, her focus initially on brief, isolated, tight-knit clusters with abstract flurries from Niggenkemper’s bass and the randomizing knitwork of Liavik Solberg. When Butcher initially enters on soprano saxophone, the random patterns generally coalesce into a continuous stream of different rhythms and complementary densities before the work’s ultimately gradual disappearance.

items.body:
Gerry Hemingway leads a band of globe-trotters: German multi-reedist Frank Gratkowski whose recorded in the US often; pianist Izumi Kimura based in Ireland; Swiss bassist Christian Weber who’s recorded on three continents, crossing paths along the way with Yanks Oliver Lake, Ellery Eskelin, Nate Wooley, and Russ Johnson; Gerry himself, based in Lucerne since 2009.

In many ways Hemingway’s contemporary music mines his time in Anthony Braxton’s wondrous 1985-1993 quartet. The leaping staccato melody with asymmetrical phrases near the top of the 36-minute “Bau 4 Assembly” is one marker; another, the way that loose suite and the 23-minute “Slivers” use long improvised sections to tie together occasional scored episodes – not that Braxton was alone in that. And Braxton’s quartet prompted Hemingway’s duo with bandmate Marilyn Crispell, prefiguring his duo with Kimura in recent years.

On the CD, a six-minute Hemingway-Kimura improvisation is sandwiched between the long pieces, but I tend to cue up that “Third Story Variation” first, for its unbeatable interplay. The pianist and drummer catch and ride the same pulse, leaving plenty of air but also knowing how to fill various spaces along the way. Their timbral senses are fully compatible: her under-the-hood preparations tilt her sound drumward. They’ll set up a slow groove together, then she’ll use her other hand to play against it. It’s all very attentive and effective.

The longer pieces credited to Hemingway unfold like narratives, with discreet episodes, varied pacing, subgroup subplots, ways to build and dispel tension. “Slivers” is for trio, minus piano, Gratkowski leading off on squawky bass clarinet, tracked by Weber’s bass; the time feel is notably looser than the duo’s. A few minutes in, bass clarinet exits, and Frank’s re-entrance on disembodied wispy alto is placed just right: an instant orchestrator’s decision. Later there’s a section for low bass clarinet and arco bass in frictive unison under free drum rustle – suggesting Braxton’s love of the sub-basement, and the flexible trio dynamic of Gerry’s early/longtime vehicle BassDrumBone. But “Slivers” does slack off a bit between the scored tentpoles. There are times you wish the drummer would apply a firmer hand in a what-would-Billy-Higgins-do kind of way. One of Gerry’s signatures at the traps is a free-swinging–arms sense of relaxation, hitting the skins as if on the rebound, with some hits maybe dropped or delayed in transit. In the closing minutes, and on the closing theme, he can come off like someone who thinks he’s swinging harder than he is.

All four assemble for “Bau 4 Assembly” which makes up the bulk of the program. The venue Bau 4 in Altbüron, Switzerland was founded by folks in the timber business, and is located in their commercial compound. In tribute, Gerry and company play or use as beaters wood scraps retrieved from the workshop, notably heard around 10 minutes in, on a fast irregular clacky and texturally light colloquy which develops into something like pointillism with a groove (no small achievement) before flute and pedal-down piano soften things up. But not for long; in very short order, a scrapwood and piano gamelan. Midway, there’s a long-tone chapter with clarinet, and Gerry singing wavery lines into his cymbals or (says here) through metal objects, an odd effect he just about pulls off. (There’s a little Robert Wyatt in his vocal wah-wahs.) The composer and the quartet cover much ground. Elsewhere, a slow line’s melodic contours are subtly mirrored by the drums.

We won’t catalog every change-up or chapter, but near the end there’s a free-jazz blowout whose presence feels like checking a box – which is not to overlook Frank’s rapid multiphonic growls. (He’s got a great command of altissimo and pressurized reed textures.) Then they break into a loose brisk tempo, to frame that free-jazz energy. It arrives just where a non-drummer’s band would place a climactic the drum solo. Then a feint toward the Braxtonian head from half an hour earlier. A few staccato hits end things without a big fuss.

items.body:
There is a substantial list of attributes that sets Ran Blake apart from every other innovative pianist of the past sixty-plus years, each of which falls under one of two headings: his choice of materials and his treatments of them. The former is based on Blake’s ability to hear connections between materials for which “disparate” is an inadequate descriptor. Who else would sequence Max Roach’s “Mendacity” and “Saving All My Love for You” – or “On Top of Old Smokey” and Michel Legrand’s “Watch What Happens”? Nobody, because what Blake does is unique. He doesn’t interpret materials as much as administer an MRI, revealing the connective tissues and vital organs as vividly, if not more so, than the skeletal structure. In the process, Blake makes the familiar sound radically new.

Blake’s collaborations with singers are central to his work. The current critical consensus is that his groundbreaking work with Jeanne Lee overshadows everything since, the respective qualities of notables like Christine Correa and Sara Serpa notwithstanding. Roots & Byways circumvents the edifice The Newest Sound Around has become, primarily because Dominique Eade takes a different tact. She is not as rooted as Correa – or Lee, for that matter – in Billie Holiday, and she is not as committed to understatement as Serpa. Like both Correa and Serpa, Eade can shape a song syllable by syllable and render a highly personal interpretation. It is Eade’s palpably deep joy in singing that sets her apart, one that is not only bursting at the seams on showstoppers like the Whitney Houston megahit, but one that even seeps into noirish songs like Mingus’ “Portrait.” It is the key to her relatability and appeal, and to that of the album, as well.

items.body: ‘What the Fog’ is the second outing for the collaborative pairing of David Allred and Peter Broderick. The compositions on the 45-minute release from the Dauw label extracted from a soundtrack to an 11-hour documentary called #monalisa that shows a day in the life of the Louvre in Paris as people engage in art, crowds, and technology – and in that order. The film feels like a balance of recognising the disconnect that exists between those engaging in art in a commercial space – a disconnect that seems further exasperated when technology adds another layer of removal. But it is also a recognition of those quiet, shared moments of human connection because of, and sometimes in spite of the art, that seemingly gives the space its meaning. Musically, Allred and Broderick are up to the task of elevating the narrative and emotional are of that lived experience. ‘What the Fog’ Begins with an ending. An almost mournful one at that. Where the film feels like a proper opening, slowly easing us into its world, the music feels like it could just as equally be an outro. “The Foghorn” opens with digital ether and then a trumpet enters, playing out like a military sendoff in a way. There’s a sort of lamenting to these early notes. Slowly, washes of distortion undulate beneath it all, letting the trumpet melody drift away. But, as piano enters, an inviting calm and reflection begins to take hold. And when the trumpet rejoins the piano, this time the piece feels more ruddered. Second piece “Cloud clearing” is bright and brief. Broderick’s lilting piano work invites us to stay in that place of calm a little further. “Stasis Oasis” sounds like it’s title – rutted and lumbering. But this contrast with piece 2 shows how Allred and Broderick can quickly strike to the heart of a moment and immerse the listener. The piece teases a tension between optimism and defeat. “Sky Swamp” undulates with slow piano strikes, over a haze of ethereal electronics. Piano chords play in slow motion creating suspense throughout – like an emotional metronome, measuring feeling at a few bpm. The synths flower above, as if waiting for the signal to shift or decay. “Crystal Flower” returns to some of the tones of “Oasis Stasis”. Eventually, vapour trails of trumpet float by in the background as sci-fi like sounds whiz by – almost alluding the dystopian dynamics of a crowd immersed in personal technology rather than communal art. Sonically, the piece feels like a new layer to the overall composition. And the once mournful trumpet seems more vivacious almost ready to transform, but it is buried in the background as if trying to fight its way through the mirage of technological decay. “Deep Dark” is as murky as it sounds. Deep in darkness with barely a shred of light. It’s feeling almost all consuming. “Shadow Diver” opens in a circulating wash of distortion. As piano and trumpet enter, hope returns. But it moves at a slow pace as if exhausted by all that has come before. Drums enter, settling into a groove – but it’s a haunted one that provides a sense of progress in the face of exhaustion. Closer “Outer Lands” with slow swaths of synths – the album is never afraid to play with and tease sci-fi tropes. But as it unfolds, it evolves into a piano-driven piece. And by the end, there is nothing but a lone piano to end things. It’s bittersweet – cautiously hopeful but somehow exhausted from the journey. All totaled, “What the Fog” comes in around 45 minutes – a snap shot of the larger film. But as a contained narrative unto itself, it tells a full story with a beginning, a middle, and an end. It’s an evocative journey with layers that will keep the listener coming back, likely more immersed on each return. What The Fog by Allred & Broderick www.dauw.bandcamp.com

items.body: Tomoyoshi Date and Stijn Huwels are experts of the minimal. Both musicians are known for their collaborative affairs – Tomoyoshi as part of Illuha, Opitope, and Melodia, and Hüwels with Norihito Suda, Danny Clay, and James Murray as part of Silent Vigils. Their releases have appeared on such highly-esteemed labels as Dauw, Eilean, 12k, and Home Normal. Both have a passion for minimalism. With hochu-ekki-tou (April 19, Home Normal), the pair conjure a long-lasting minimal atmosphere, running from the first second to the last drop. The pair complement one another to perfect degrees: both have a deep fascination for the art, maintaining the structure with delicate hands and soft tweaks which ebb, flow, and glow. They not only keep the music interesting, but they do it without jeopardising the drone’s sanctity, not wanting to deliberately interfere with its natural course and direction but adding tiny parts every now and then to the overall web of sound. It’s somewhat of a balancing act. The sound must be fed in stages so as to keep it from going stale, to add colour, shade, and interest, but add too much and you run the risk of decaying its minimal foundations. Patience is key. In some ways, minimal music is music of starvation. It requires the listener to go deeper, to go beneath its surface. Its lack of any real change is a crucial part of its self and its priceless beauty. It draws the musician towards it, pulling them into its sphere like a magnet. Then, and only then, does it reveal itself to be music of incredible depth, the opposite of a hunger, revealing well-fed, intensely satisfying music. The tracks are naturally long, as they need the space to develop and unwind, stretching their legs. This is a record of deep listening, and its slow-moving development never for a second stops it from being interesting or immediate. Minimalism involves a close-up shot, after all. There’s a nice parallel, a sweet contradiction, to the track, ‘ekki’, where sharp details come to the fore. Chips and scars come into view thanks to its high definition. A muted piano contradicts this proximity with a series of distant thumps, fingers treading over keys, coming from another part of the house and passing as if through thick walls. Looking at something in the distance will render it blurry. But something that’s extremely close can also appear blurred. The melody is like a whirlpool, slinking into the lower register and its inky depths, gradually expanding to take in more sounds. Adding gentle electric guitar melodies and the purifying sound of running water, coda ‘tou’ is tranquil and involving, bringing the listener into a secret place and helping to clear the mind of its worry-creases. The guitar’s tone is fragile, changing as it rings out. Together, the pair make exceptional minimal music. You wouldn’t want anyone else. www.homenormal.bandcamp.com

items.body: A sea without a port “Life springs from death, just like the sun rises each morning after its nightly voyage to the heavenly plain.” Anyone who knows Joseph Sannicandro from his work on A Closer Listen, will know that he’s not someone who will take anything at face value, but likes to dig around and uncover the background stories behind any releases he might be writing about, outlining motivations and socio-political connections, which allow him to draw up illuminating interviews with artists. He’s seldom off duty and when he goes off to Mexico City (or el DF) he takes his digital recorder with him, much in the same way that a XIX traveller might’ve carried a sketchbook jotting things down, taking notes, outlining the aural world he encounters in a bid to unpack its complexities. And yet he is wise enough to recognise himself as an American tourist with all the cumbersome baggage that comes with it. In the extensive linear notes to A Sea Without A Port, Sannicandro states, “As our southern neighbor, there is the uncomfortable fact that so much of what is now the USA was once Mexico, the forgotten/repressed/unknown fact that much of the Mexican-American war was fought because Mexico had outlawed slavery. The fact that European settlement was forced on the indigenous peoples. Bigots and TV pundits cultivate fear of ‘illegal’ immigrants, yet ironically Mexico has long been perceived as a place where American ruffians and outlaws could flee to escape justice.” It follows that one of the tracks is titled “El tratado de Guadalupe” denying any possibility that this could ever be interpreted as a picture postcard rendition of DF. However, Sannicandro is neither descriptive nor dogmatic in his approach. “The post-colonial Mexico, the Mexico rocked by the effects of NAFTA, of sprawling slums and terrible poverty, of colonized peoples and traditional ways of life obliterated by the violence of multinational corporations and agricultural subsidies” are all acknowledged but never color our listening experience. Rather, it’s cultural filters that are used to ease our way into the complex sonic territory. The opening track, “I dreamt I was dreaming and I came home too late,” is titled after poetry by Roberto Bolaño. Aside from friends and musical connections (Umor Rex), Sannicandro is quick in paying tribute to the work of Juan Villoro, Leon Trotsky, Frida Kahlo, Francis Alÿs, Alejandro González Iñárritu, Octavio Paz, Rufino Tamayo and all the artists and writers who introduced him to DF long before he physically set foot there. And yet A Sea Without a Port never feels like the result of thoroughly researched homework. It is never dry, on the contrary, it sizzles with stimuli. Sannicandro is not interested in adopting an observational stance. He happily tampers with field recordings preferring the textural to the documentary. He clearly has fun with whatever is picked up by both his Tascam DR-05 and his iPhone 3GS and is unafraid to compromise the supposed integrity of the untreated material. Presumably, in order not to be overwhelmed by the task at hand, he breaks down any possible linear narrative into disjointed chapters, often opting for jump cuts rather than cross fades. He’s constantly revising, retracing lines, rubbing out and filling in the gaps with new contradictory aural impressions, abruptly stopping the flow of sound almost mid sentence to introduce startling pauses. Chubby Cheker’s Let’s Twist Again filters through the fuzzy sonic ambience of the title track, snippets of lines from popular TV dramas populate “Ivan Illich”, short tape loops of street hawking play over and over like broken records on “Non-aerial cartography”, reverb blasts through “A halo is antiquated”. Everything is fragmented, shaken up and eventually blended to produce an intoxicating auditory mixture extracted from the city’s nooks and crannies. Over the last 20 seconds of the last track, “The tragic concision of the dream”, Sannicandro introduces another snippet of what could be perceived as quintessentially “traditional Mexican music” but frustrates any expectations one might have of finally having time to savour its melodic quality by unceremoniously dropping the tune after only 10 seconds or so, leaving us with nothing to hold onto, and the impossibility of grasping yet again the “characteristic Mexican spirit” of his chosen location. As Sannicandro explains, “These recordings acknowledge the impossibility of ever truly knowing a place, especially one as rich and complex and contradictory as el DF.” A Sea Without a Port is out as free digital download on Galaverna. a sea without a port by Joseph Sannicandro www.noiseeconomy.wordpress.com www.soundcloud.com/thenewobjective

items.body:
After the OĽUN album I reviewed enthusiastically a while back, here’s the next project, again motivated and led by violinist/fiddler/composer Ján Kružliak Jr., continuing the rapprochement, indeed embrace, between Slovakia’s traditional music and its classical music. This time it reconnects the works of classical composers who were inspired by and drew on village musics with those traditional sources and styles.
Three ensembles are involved: the Spectrum Quartett led by Kru�liak with two violins, viola and cello; Nogaband, the traditional-style quartet of fiddles, contra (chording viola) and bass that’s led by fiddler and singer Michal Noga; and the female vocal group Ulijanky, plus guest singer Simona Hulejov�.
The majority of the tracks are interpretations of works by Slovak composer Eugen Suchon (1908-1993), with others from fellow-Slovaks Ilja Zeljenka (1932-2007) and Alexander Moyzes (1906-1984), and Hungarian B�la Bart�k (1881-1945) who did a lot of his very detailed collecting of folk music in Slovakia.
In each case the sources - musicians and locations in villages across Slovakia - are credited in the notes, and these arrangements and performances reconnect with the energy and traditional vocal sound of those sources.
In no way is this an orchestra-smoothed thing; this is gutsy, brilliantly played and sung music with all the spirit, skill and technique of traditional music, from players and singers who deeply understand and inhabit it. It’s a glorious piece of work, music to luxuriate in. There’s too much richness to begin to detail, but here’s a dip into a few moments to give the flavor. The tracks all have very long titles detailing their sources, so for brevity’s sake I’ll just give track numbers.

items.body: Karine Polwart has proved herself to be an exceptional talent as a singer and songwriter for many years, all the way back to her time with Malinky (the song �Thaney� was a revelation). As a solo artist she�s grown and continually expanded her horizons, coming now to Windblown , a project that began life seven years ago, when Polwart, along with sound designer and composer Pippa Murphy, was artist in residence at Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh. The album, with its stage show and book, tells the story of the garden�s oldest specimen, a Sabal palm tree ( Sabal bermudana ), which was gently felled in 2021, and contained a surprise nobody had expected. The tree is the starting point. From there, imagination runs free. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan It�s an album of voice and piano (the outstanding, sympathetic Dave Milligan), and, for all its global outlook on connections, one that�s very rooted in Scotland. You can hear it on the opening track, �Hear The Rigging/Last In Line,� where the melody becomes a slow, aching lament that would sound completely natural on the pipes. The stripped-down sound gives the songs both crafted stateliness and real intimacy. Each one is an exhalation, a memory, a celebration and exploration, with recurring phrases in the words and music acting as touchstones � or even hooks; they certainly stick in the mind. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan In many ways, this is a modest album, with piano, voice and light, judicious soundscaping. It won�t overpower with noise. Yet at the same time, it�s epic, a look at history, at the flow and grandeur of nature, and the things we all carry within us. The music, and especially Polwart�s warm, compassionate voice, envelop the listener, and makes them a participant, not an observer, but a part of the journey and the history. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan The irony arrives at the end, when the venerable old tree is down, and seeds are examined. What people for two hundred years had believed to be a Sabal bermudana turns out to be something different, a Sabal mexicana � and one of the small plants fill grow where it�s forerunner once stood. Windblown by Karine Polwart & Pippa Murphy featuring Dave Milligan Like music, plants keep to a different time � and this album/book/show give the tree the requiem it deserves, as well as hope for the future. Find the artist online. Sara Serpa - Encounters and Collisions (Review) Karine Polwart- Laws of Motion (Review) Live in the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh, 2025

items.body: Sudan Dudan is a Norwegian duo, Marit Karlberg and Anders Erik R�ine, who have released four albums over the last twenty years. On M�rke refrenger , their fifth, they are joined by Hans Hulb�kmo and Magnus Skavhaug Nergaard, contributing instrumentally and with the production. There are eight songs on the album with accompaniment principally led by acoustic guitar, augmented by fiddles, langeleik, lyre, jaws harp and more. The opening track, �Gard og grind� (�Fence and gate�) is a fine introduction to what is to come: finger-picked acoustic guitar, fiddle, bass and snare-drum played with brushes leading into the harmonized vocal, together creating an alluring sound drawing the listener in. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The mood of the album, reflected in its title which translates as �Dark Refrains,� is not always dark, but most of the material, including the title track, certainly has a reflective quality. According to the press release �the lyrics smoulder with unease about the present and the future, while looking back to the myths and riddles of the past. They speak of the earth, the sun, the moon, stars and planets, of lost brothers, quarrelling sisters, loss and grief, of the power of imagination, and of the answers to the simplest and most difficult riddles.� The lyrics of all the songs, in Norwegian, are included in the sleeve notes and while a hasty online translation can aid with some understanding, the full meanings tend to remain cryptic, but there is a sense that words and music complement each other. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan For all its dark moodiness, M�rke refrenger does have its lighter moments. �Bagatelle� recalls and reinvents the melody of a well-known French song, adding some off-kilter harmonies, while �Rulleball� is more characteristically Norwegian, employing a vocal style known as tralling in which words are replaced by a vocalization of the melody, originally used to accompany dances when no instrument was available. No translation necessary there. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The final track �Skriften p� veggen� (�the writing on the wall�) features, for the only time on the album, electric guitar. The sound is deep and twangy, shades of Duane Eddy or a David Lynch soundtrack and it works very well. All in all a fine, imaginatively conceived and beautifully produced record, available as a download or vinyl. Find the artists online. items.body:
Though this recording documents the work of thirteen of Belgium's most innovative ensembles, the real star is the Park Abbey located just outside Leuven and founded in 1129. Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,
La Pump
rhythms, and accordion-based
bal-musette
flavors.
For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. They have rendered a warm sound using the natural reverb of ancient stone provided by the project�s silent partner.

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items.body:
According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

items.body:
The musical partnership between Kalaniemi and Alakotila has thrived over a remarkable 35 years, long enough to the Finnish pair to develop a stunning intimacy and telepathy. Kalaniemi is a lovingly melodic accordion player, with a sharp ear for a good tune, building each one into a thing of great beauty, while pianist Alakotila not only supports her but adds enough of his own to help transform every piece into a glistening gem.
There�s a sense of calmness to the work here, a long, sweet exhalation between two instrumentalists who are deep enough in sync to allow seamless improvisation beyond any written score and carry the listeners along with them. For much of the album, it�s just the pair of them, including Kalaniemi�s wordless voice, as on the opener, the tradional �Lyck�nskan.� She does charmingly sing lyrics on the title track, written by Lasse M�rtenson, with the sound there neatly and sparingly expanded with the addition of a string quartet.
Morgondimma
There are several original pieces alongside the tradition, with Kalaniemi�s �Hambo Vid F�bodan� a real standout, and it�s perhaps inevitable on any disc featuring accordion that a Piazzolla tune should be included, brings its own shadows to the whole (�Oblivion�). And, this being Finland, a tango is almost obligatory, in this case Alakotila�s �Tango Berlin.�
Tango Berlin
There�s a gentle, dreamlike quality to so much of this, flowing and mellifluous. The pieces aren�t an arena for showy virtuosity. Instead, the two musicians serve the tune, exploring and genuinely enjoying their performances.
It won�t shake the earth, but it makes for some true listening beauty.

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors.
